title: Just another copy and paste? Comparing the security vulnerabilities of ChatGPT generated code and StackOverflow answers
authors: Sivana Hamer, Marcelo d’Amorim, Laurie Williams

reading.body:
ChatGPT-generated Java code carried about 20 percent fewer security weaknesses than code copied from StackOverflow, but neither source was clean.

The study compared 108 Java snippets per platform using CodeQL. ChatGPT code held 248 weakness instances, StackOverflow answers held 302, and ChatGPT produced 19 distinct weakness types against StackOverflow's 22. Across both sources the researchers counted 274 unique vulnerabilities spanning 25 types. The gap is real and statistically significant, but the absolute numbers matter more than the ranking: hundreds of weaknesses in a few hundred snippets means insecure code is the norm in both channels.

For AI specifically, the finding cuts against the assumption that generated code arrives safer than the human-written code it replaces. It does not. The improvement is marginal relative to the volume of defects, and the overlap in weakness types suggests both sources fail in similar ways. Code generation is a compute-bound capability that scales with the same infrastructure as everything else, but its output quality on security does not scale with it.

What this does not cover: the data is Java only, drawn from security-related StackOverflow questions, which likely overstates defect density relative to ordinary code. It says nothing about whether developers actually ship these snippets, and nothing about runtime exposure. It also predates any model newer than the one tested in 2024.

explain_beginner: This paper compares code that people copy from two places: answers on StackOverflow and code written by ChatGPT. The researchers took 108 Java code snippets from each source and checked them for known security weaknesses. ChatGPT's code had 248 weaknesses, while StackOverflow's had 302, so ChatGPT did somewhat better, about 20 percent fewer. But both had many problems, and together they showed 274 unique weaknesses of 25 different kinds. The lesson is simple: code copied from anywhere, whether written by a person or an AI, should not be trusted without checking, and good development habits are needed to reduce risk.
explain_business: Most developers now use generative AI in their workflow, and many still copy code from sites like StackOverflow. This study checked Java snippets from both sources and found security weaknesses in each: ChatGPT code had 248, StackOverflow had 302, so AI did modestly better but was far from clean. The practical takeaway is that no copied code, human or AI written, can be trusted as is. Decisions this informs include investing in code review, static analysis, and secure coding training rather than assuming AI tools remove risk, and treating AI assistance as one input among several that still needs verification.
explain_practitioner: The authors reused a Java dataset of security-related StackOverflow questions and answers, posed the same questions to ChatGPT, and collected the generated code. After curating, they analyzed 108 snippets per platform with CodeQL, counting Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) instances and types. ChatGPT code contained 248 vulnerabilities versus 302 in StackOverflow snippets, a statistically significant 20 percent reduction. ChatGPT also produced 19 CWE types against StackOverflow's 22. Across both sources, 274 unique vulnerabilities and 25 CWE types appeared. The authors conclude that copied code from either platform requires standard secure engineering practices, and that future work should target reducing insecure code propagation.
